text: A Service gives a changing set of Pods one stable virtual IP, but that alone doesn't solve a second problem: something still has to tell every other Pod what that IP actually is. Hard-coding it defeats the whole point. The real answer is DNS — every Service also gets a predictable name, and any Pod in the cluster resolves that name the same way your laptop resolves a website.

That name has four pieces, read left to right: the Service's own name, payments-api; the namespace it lives in, billing; a fixed segment, svc, meaning this is a Service record; and cluster.local, the cluster's internal DNS domain. Put together, payments-api.billing.svc.cluster.local resolves to that Service's stable ClusterIP — the same address from the Services lesson — which kube-proxy then routes to a real, current Pod.

CoreDNS is the server that actually answers these lookups — running in-cluster, almost always in kube-system, fronted by its own Service conventionally still named kube-dns. It watches the API for Services and Endpoints and keeps its records in sync automatically. You never hand-edit a zone file; create a Service, and CoreDNS already knows how to answer for it.

Kubernetes configures every Pod's DNS search path to include its own namespace first, which is why a Pod inside billing can reach payments-api with no suffix at all. Call from a different namespace, like checkout, and that shortcut disappears — the bare name would try to resolve inside checkout first and likely fail, or worse, match an unrelated Service of the same name sitting there. Cross-namespace config should always use at least the service.namespace form.

When a name won't resolve, don't guess — spin up a throwaway debug Pod and test it directly. nslookup against the full name confirms whether CoreDNS answers at all and what IP comes back, which you compare against kubectl get svc to confirm it matches the real ClusterIP. Checking /etc/resolv.conf inside that same Pod shows you exactly which search path Kubernetes configured, which is usually the actual explanation.

Every example so far has quietly assumed that any Pod can call any Service it can resolve — there's been nothing stopping a Pod in one part of the cluster from reaching a Service in a completely different, unrelated part. Next lesson is where that assumption gets challenged: NetworkPolicy resources, which restrict pod-to-pod traffic by label selector instead of leaving the cluster wide open by default.
